title: My brother's keeper (Genesis 4:9–16)
hook: Cain asks "Am I my brother's keeper?" and the rest of the Torah answers him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cain and Abel: two offerings, and a jealousy God warned about before it struck. Your line was it crouches at the door. Did you catch one jealous thought and give it a name? Day thirty-one.

Cain comes back from the field alone. Two brothers went out; one walks home. And God asks him a question, the way God asked Adam in the garden, a question God already knows the answer to. In the old JPS translation: "Where is Abel thy brother?" Picture a parent in a kitchen asking where the cookies went, while looking straight at the crumbs. The question isn't for information. It's a door held open. Cain could walk through it. He could say, I did something terrible. Instead he shrugs. "I know not; am I my brother's keeper?" A lie, and then a question thrown back in God's face. It's one of the most famous questions ever asked. And the story, and the whole Torah after it, spends a very long time answering it.
screen: `CAIN COMES HOME ALONE.` → `WHERE IS ABEL THY BROTHER?` → `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?`

segments.voice: The Hebrew for keeper is shomer: a guard, a watchman, someone who keeps a thing safe. It comes from the root shamar, to keep, the same root the Torah uses for keeping Shabbat. So Cain's question is sharp: am I supposed to guard him? Isn't that somebody else's job? God doesn't argue. God answers with a sound: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto Me from the ground." And the rabbis noticed something in the Hebrew. The word for blood there is plural. Bloods. The Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin, explains: not only Abel's blood, but the blood of every child and grandchild who would have come from him. Cain didn't end one life. He ended a world. That's where the famous teaching comes from, the one you met a week ago: whoever destroys a single life, it's as if they destroyed a whole world. Then comes the surprise. Cain is punished: he'll be a wanderer, the ground won't yield for him. He cries that it's too much to bear. And God puts a sign on him, so that no one who finds him will kill him. Even the murderer is kept. God answers Cain's question by doing the very thing Cain refused to do. And the rest of the Torah keeps answering. In Leviticus: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour." A few lines later: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." And the Talmud turns it into a principle: all Israel are responsible for one another. Cain asked, am I my brother's keeper? The whole tradition leans in and says: yes.
screen: `SHOMER — A GUARD, A KEEPER.` · `THE BLOOD CRIES FROM THE GROUND.` · `BLOODS: A WHOLE WORLD ENDED.` · `EVEN CAIN IS KEPT.` · then, large: `NEITHER SHALT THOU STAND IDLY BY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind a sibling, or if you don't have one, an old friend: someone who used to be close and has drifted a little. See their face. Now notice what you don't know. How are they sleeping? What's worrying them this month? When did you last ask? Don't scold yourself. Just let the question sit in you the way God's question sat in front of Cain: where is your brother? If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If you don't, hold them in your attention. The bell holds the time.
My brother's keeper. Cain's shrugging question, and the Torah's long answer: we are asked to guard one another.
Your line: yes, you are. Today, check on that sibling or old friend. One message, one call. Not to fix anything. Just to ask, and to mean it. Day thirty-one.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching draws on Cain's question and on Leviticus 19:16 to say that people are responsible for one another; the Talmud's principle that all Israel are responsible for one another is often cited when communities organize help for someone in trouble.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 4:9 ("Where is Abel thy brother?" and "I know not; am I my brother's keeper?") and 4:10 ("the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto Me from the ground").
Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Leviticus 19:16 and 19:18 as quoted.
Shomer/shamar linked to keeping Shabbat (shamor, Deuteronomy 5:12): confirm the root connection is stated fairly.

Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 reads demei (bloods, plural) in 4:10 as Abel and his potential descendants; day 24 already cited the same Mishnah for 'a whole world'. Confirm the 'one you met a week ago' callback.
Cain's words in 4:13 are paraphrased ('too much to bear') because the Hebrew avon can mean sin or punishment; JPS wording not quoted.
'All Israel are responsible for one another' (Shevuot 39a) is paraphrased; the teach applies it as 'the whole tradition'. Confirm the framing.
